source.title: Gradient descent in Gaussian random fields as a toy model for high-dimensional optimisation in deep learning
source.authors: Mariano Chouza; Stephen J. Roberts; Stefan Zohren

record.file_problem: Full paper text is supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests gradient descent on simulated Gaussian random fields and a random-field classifier toy model, with a different setup from the claim's neural-network training recipes.
record.gate_note: The results bear on gradient descent and classification, but the paper does not train the benchmark convolutional networks or study the initialization, depth, width, residual, learning-rate stability, or batch-normalization conditions in the versions. It reports test accuracy for classification; it does not report training classification error. Cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes gradient descent on Gaussian random fields and reports a toy classifier's test accuracy. Its own results do not test any V1–V6: neither one-step field improvement nor a test-accuracy collapse establishes neural-network training error, spurious minima, initialization effects, depth degradation, batch-normalization benefits, or recovery above a linearized stability limit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. More precisely, the authors derive and simulate one-step gradient-descent field-value distributions, obtain an optimal learning rate scaling as N^(-1/2), and compare expected improvement with random search and an estimated local-domain minimum. Separately, their fixed random-field classifier achieves useful synthetic and MNIST parity test accuracy. These results do not establish the neural-network mechanisms in V1–V6.
record.recipe_differences: A Gaussian random field replaces a neural network's internal parameters; the classification experiment uses minibatch gradient descent on a fixed random field and reports test accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy depends on learning rate after a critical value; the MNIST critical learning rate varies with dimensionality (η ≈ 0.13 at N = 500 and η ≈ 0.03 at N = 5000).

fits_no_version.finding: The random-field classifier exceeds 96% held-out MNIST even/odd accuracy at reported N = 5000. Accuracy collapses to random performance near learning rates 0.13 for reported N = 500 and 0.03 for N = 5000.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A fixed Gaussian random-field classifier can learn MNIST parity classification, with a dimension-dependent learning-rate ceiling for useful test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic sine-separated classification experiment compares test accuracy across random-field dimensions and learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-field classifier performance on a synthetic binary task depends on dimensionality and learning rate.

record.problems: Classification results are test accuracy rather than training error; the learning-rate curves are presented only as figures without exact values, and no uncertainty or control comparison is stated.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports theoretical and simulated results for one-step gradient descent on Gaussian random fields. Those concern field-value distributions and expected loss improvement, not training classification error or a behavior named by V1–V6, so they are not rows for these claim versions.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, including random labels, model-size effects, early stopping and regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious-local-minimum frequencies and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, deep plain tanh networks and residual training without normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Loss recovery above an initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence relative to that threshold.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Change the reader's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. Theoretical and simulated one-step results are already declared in rows_left_out and require no missing entry. The supplied text contains figure labels but does not expose readable accuracy curves, so exact figure-only values cannot be verified.

versions.untested_parts: No CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 convolutional network training, corrupted or random labels, or training classification error; only a random-field toy classifier's test accuracy is reported.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student setup or width sweep for spurious minima.
No depth or identity-shortcut comparison, and no plain tanh or unnormalized residual network experiment.
No initialization comparison or signal/gradient propagation test.
No stability-limit, curvature, or full-batch learning-rate experiment.
